_readme: THE PROVENANCE REGISTER — [pipeline B-17] Private/requirements/ (was pipeline/04-backend-platform.md, folded into the JSON spec 2026-08-15)
B-17: 'Verification against production is permitted and expected, but every artifact it creates is
provably removed, and the check is mechanical rather than remembered.'
🔴 WHY THE ORIGINAL ACCEPTANCE CRITERION WAS REPLACED. It read: 'a single command reports, per
shared table, the count of rows matching the test-marker convention — and it returns zero.' There
was no test-marker convention, so 'matches the convention' was the EMPTY PREDICATE: the count is 0
on any production state whatsoever, forever. Fill `events` with a million probe rows and it still
returns zero. The criterion was satisfied by the absence of the thing it asked to be built.
THE INVERSION. Instead of counting rows that carry a marker nobody applies, count the rows that
CANNOT BE TRACED TO A RELEASED BUILD. That set has a non-empty complement, probe rows land in it
automatically, and it does not depend on anybody remembering to tag anything.
🔴 AND 'EVERY SHARED TABLE MUST BE EMPTY' IS DEAD ON ARRIVAL. `cron_heartbeat` held 16 legitimate
production rows and `revocation_reasons` 8 seeded reference rows when this register was written.
Emptiness was never the property; ATTRIBUTABILITY is.
Because the columns differ, and pretending otherwise is how a check stops checking. Only `events`
and `consent_artifacts` carry `app_version` (0002_analytics.sql:40, :77). The other seven have no
such column and never will: they are written by the EDGE — a scheduled handler, a merchant-of-record
webhook, a route, or the migration itself — and the edge does not know a client version. So each of
those declares its own marker AND the reason that marker is the honest provenance for that table.
A single portfolio-wide rule would have had to be `app_version`, seven tables would have been exempt,
and the exemptions would have been invisible.
GATE    · tooling/ci/assert-prod-provenance.mjs — runs on every push in ci.yml. SECRETLESS, so it
CANNOT SEE PRODUCTION. It asserts only what is checkable from the repo: every table the
migrations create has a rule here, every rule names a column that table really has, every
non-`released-build` rule carries a written reason, and the monitor is wired.
MONITOR · tooling/ops/check-prod-provenance.mjs — runs daily in ops-watch.yml, which holds
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and has no push trigger. It is the ONLY limb that can see a row.
It is a WEAKER RUNG than a gate: green means 'nothing has contradicted this since the
last run', never 'this holds'.
Adding a table to services/platform/migrations/ without adding a row here FAILS THE GATE. That is
the regression this register exists to catch — B-17's prose named four shared tables and the
migrations create nine, three days apart.

resolvers.released-build: The marker value must be the version string of a build the release lane actually shipped: `<release_line>.<run_number>+<sha7>`, where a SERVED lane in tooling/channel-register.json has a SUCCESSFUL run numbered <run_number> whose head commit is <sha7>. Derived from the GitHub Actions API at read time — never a list in this file. `dev` (the dart-define default), `c6-localprobe` (the C-6 live probe's literal) and NULL all fail, which is the point.
resolvers.live-environment: The marker value must be exactly `live`. Every row in these tables is written by the money rail, which stamps `live` or `sandbox` on purpose ([5]M-12: a sandbox notification is stored so it is auditable and can never write a live entitlement). A verification against production necessarily runs in sandbox, so `sandbox` IS the test marker for this half of the schema — and NULL is worse than either, because it is a row the rail could not attribute at all.
resolvers.cron-job: The marker value must be a job the deployed Worker both DECLARES and USES — the `export const <NAME>_JOB = '<literal>'` set in services/platform/src, the same derivation tooling/ops/check-heartbeats.mjs uses for its completeness limb. A heartbeat row naming a job no deployed code writes is residue from a renamed or deleted job.
resolvers.provider-register: The marker value must be a rail declared in tooling/legal/provider-register.json. A row naming a provider the register does not carry is either a fabricated row or a rail that reached production without a legal record, and both need a human.
resolvers.migration-seed: The marker value must be one of the literals the migrations themselves INSERT into that column. These are reference rows, not data: their provenance is the migration ledger, and any value outside it was put there by hand.
resolvers.app-catalogue: The marker value must be the slug of an app the factory actually ships, read from tooling/channel-register.json's `apps` list — the same catalogue assert-channel-register.mjs grades its own rows against, never a second list here. For DERIVED tables that carry no build marker of their own. ⚠️ DELIBERATELY WEAKER THAN `released-build`, AND IT SAYS SO: it proves the row belongs to a real app, not that a released build wrote it, so a row derived from a `dev`-stamped event still resolves. That residual is accepted only because the SOURCE table is separately held to `released-build`, and it is recorded here rather than hidden. What it does catch is the state this portfolio has actually produced — rows for an app id nothing ships, i.e. probe residue (`c6-localprobe`).

events.reason: Carries `app_version` (0002_analytics.sql:40), written straight through from the client envelope by services/platform/src/routes/events.ts. This is the nearest thing to a marker that already existed — C-6's live probe rows carried `app_version: c6-localprobe` — which is why the inversion is cheap here.

consent_artifacts.reason: Carries `app_version` (0002_analytics.sql:77), same writer, same envelope. Append-only by design, so a stray row can never be corrected by an UPDATE — it can only be deleted, which is exactly the disposition B-17 wants proven.

entitlements.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN AND NEVER WILL HAVE ONE: the row is written by services/platform/src/lib/mor/store.ts from a merchant-of-record notification, not by a client, so no app build is involved and there is no version to record. `provider_environment` (0004_money_rail.sql:73) is the column that answers the same question — which money world produced this row. It is the highest-consequence table in the set: B-17's own first-revenue note is that a test entitlement row in production is a free Pro unlock nobody notices, and a NULL here is precisely such a row.

cron_heartbeat.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the Worker's own scheduled handler (services/platform/src/scheduled.ts), which has no client and no app build. `job` is its only self-describing column, and it is a closed set the source declares. THIS TABLE IS WHY 'shared tables must be empty' had to be abandoned — its 16 rows are the instrument working, not residue.

provider_notifications.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the MoR webhook (0004 section B) before anything interprets it. `environment` (0004_money_rail.sql:161) is stamped by the rail itself. This is the one non-pseudonymous store in platform_db — it keeps the buyer's name, email and billing country VERBATIM — so a sandbox row lingering here is a real person's data retained for no reason, not just untidiness.

provider_accounts.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN and no `environment` column either: the row is DERIVED from a notification rather than received, so the environment lives on the notification it was derived from. `provider` is the column it does carry, and it is a closed set the legal register owns. The row links a person to a subscription, which is why it deliberately carries `user_id` and joins the erasure sweep.

unclaimed_payments.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the webhook when money arrived and no account could be resolved. `environment` (0004_money_rail.sql) is stamped by the rail. A sandbox row here is the most misleading kind of residue in the whole schema — it is evidence of an unresolved real payment, and a fake one wastes exactly the investigation the table exists to make possible.

cancellation_requests.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN: written by the cancellation route (0005) from the authenticated session, not from an app envelope. `environment` is NOT NULL in the DDL for the same [5]M-12 reason as the rest of the rail, so the marker is guaranteed present and only its VALUE can be wrong.

revocation_reasons.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN and no writer at all: this is REFERENCE DATA seeded by 0004_money_rail.sql:282 and extended only by an additive INSERT in a later migration. Nothing in the running system writes it, so 'traced to a released build' is the wrong question — the right one is 'is this row in the migration ledger'. Its 8 rows are the second reason emptiness could never have been the rule.

events_daily.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN — the rollup DROPS it, deliberately: 0007_events_rollup.sql keeps only the five grain columns the [11]E-11 numbers need, and the build string is not one of them. So the strongest marker is genuinely absent rather than waived, and `app_id` is the only self-describing column that survives aggregation. 🔴 THE TEMPTING RULE HERE WAS 'provenance is INHERITED from `events`', and it was rejected because NO ROW COULD EVER VIOLATE IT — an assertion that cannot fail inflates the covered-table count while checking nothing, which is worse than declaring none. `app-catalogue` can fail: a row whose `app_id` names no shipped app is probe residue.

rollup_state.reason: NO `app_version` COLUMN and no app at all: this is a CONTROL, not data — one row naming the last day the rollup fully consumed, which the events sweep reads to decide how far it may delete. 0007_events_rollup.sql seeds the only legitimate value (`events_daily`) with an INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so the migration ledger IS its provenance and 'traced to a released build' is the wrong question, exactly as it is for revocation_reasons one entry up. A `rollup` value outside the seeded set was put there by hand.
